all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, imports from `bench.dm._immune`. The task boundary explicitly names `DetectorDiagnosis` as part of the immune response layer, but the shim sources `DetectorDiagnosis` from `_types.py` rather than from `_immune.py`. That split may be valid internally, but the artifact gives no stable ownership signal for the diagnosis API: the docstring says `_immune.py` is the “immune detection layer,” while the diagnosis type central to that layer is exported from `_types.py`. This creates an interface-location ambiguity for consumers and reviewers trying to map where immune diagnoses are defined and maintained. Evidence: `from bench.dm._types import ... DetectorDiagnosis ...`; `from bench.dm._immune import DetectorHealthMonitor` only.  

FIX:  
Clarify ownership in the module inventory docstring so the exported location of `DetectorDiagnosis` matches the documented decomposition.

<<<<
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses (all shared vocabulary)
    _immune.py             DetectorHealthMonitor (immune detection layer)
====
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses (all shared vocabulary,
                           including DetectorDiagnosis)
    _immune.py             DetectorHealthMonitor (immune detection layer)
>>>>

FOLLOW:  
- This does not change runtime imports, but it removes a review and maintenance ambiguity around where diagnosis schema changes belong.  
- If the intent was instead for `DetectorDiagnosis` to live in `_immune.py`, then the stronger downstream fix is a code move plus import adjustment. The artifact does not justify asserting that relocation, so the documentation correction is the closed-form safe fix.  
- This also helps align type ownership for any future `__all__` or API docs generation.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Amend the module inventory docstring to state explicitly that `DetectorDiagnosis` is defined in `_types.py`.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, immune layer export section versus analytical boundary. The boundary includes “immune config parameters,” but the shim exports only the aggregate `DynamicManagementConfig` type and provides no documentation that the immune parameters are part of that type’s public compatibility surface. Because the file is a compatibility shim, failing to identify which config fields are relied upon by the immune layer makes the immune interface incomplete at the module-contract level. Evidence from artifact: docstring inventory for `_types.py` is generic; no mention of immune fields such as `immune_feedback_enabled`, `immune_damping_rounds`, `timeout_multiplier`, `theta_under`, `n_fail`, `persistence_window`, `eta_underperform`, `k_min`, `max_per_model_directive_chars`.  

FIX:  
Document that immune parameters are part of the exported config contract.

<<<<
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses (all shared vocabulary)
====
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses (all shared vocabulary,
                           including immune config parameters on
                           DynamicManagementConfig)
>>>>

FOLLOW:  
- This fix improves boundary completeness for review and for downstream callers constructing config objects.  
- It does not solve any missing runtime symbol issue because the config fields are attribute-level, not module-level names.  
- If separate generated docs exist, they must be updated to enumerate the immune fields explicitly; otherwise the ambiguity remains outside this file.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Extend the `_types.py` inventory line to state that `DynamicManagementConfig` includes the immune config parameters used by the immune subsystem.

all_findings.description: FIND: `DetectorDiagnosis` is listed in the analytical boundary as a core immune component, yet the shim imports it from `bench.dm._types` under the "Types, config, enums, dataclasses" section — not under the "Immune layer" section. Every other immune boundary component (`DetectorHealthMonitor`, `FailureHandler`) is grouped under the immune heading. This organizational misclassification means a reviewer scanning the shim for the immune API surface will not find `DetectorDiagnosis` where expected. FOLLOW: Downstream, any automated import-graph analysis or dependency audit scoped to the "Immune layer" comment block will miss `DetectorDiagnosis` entirely. If the shim is later refactored to split sections into separate `__init__` files or conditional imports, `DetectorDiagnosis` will not travel with the immune components.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Move the `DetectorDiagnosis` import from the `_types` block into the "Immune layer" block (it can still be imported from `_types.py` at the module level — the grouping is for human and tooling clarity). Alternatively, add a comment in the types block: `# Also part of immune boundary — see analytical boundary`.

all_findings.description: FIND: The interface summary (Section 1) lists `convergence_detector._novel_classes(r)` as a function called by `process_round()`. The leading underscore marks this as a private method of `ConvergenceDetector`. The immune integration in `process_round()` therefore depends on an internal implementation detail of a component outside the immune boundary. FOLLOW: If `ConvergenceDetector` is refactored and `_novel_classes` is renamed, inlined, or removed, the immune integration breaks silently — there is no interface contract protecting this call. Every other convergence-detector method called by the immune path (`kappa`, `converged`, `get_cumulative_classes`) is public. This one is not.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Promote `_novel_classes` to a public method `novel_classes(r)` on `ConvergenceDetector`, or add a public accessor that delegates to it. Update `process_round()` to call the public name.

all_findings.description: FIND: The interface summary (Section 2) lists `self._pre_fix_snapshots` as a write-only mutable state: immune writes config snapshots before adjustments. No read interface, restore method, or rollback mechanism is documented anywhere in the interface summary. Snapshots without a consumer are dead state — they consume memory proportional to the number of immune adjustments but serve no documented purpose. FOLLOW: If the intent is rollback capability, the absence of a restore path means the immune layer can damage config (e.g., lower `tau_sim` too aggressively) with no recovery mechanism other than restarting the session. If the intent is audit logging, `_immune_adjustments` already serves that role, making `_pre_fix_snapshots` redundant.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Either (a) add a `restore_snapshot(idx)` method and document when it should be called (e.g., when a remediation is later found harmful), or (b) remove `_pre_fix_snapshots` and ensure `_immune_adjustments` captures old/new values for audit.

all_findings.description: FIND: The interface summary (Section 2) shows immune can write to `self.config.pre_decompose_models` (a `Set[str]`) by adding models. No removal interface is documented. This creates a one-way ratchet: once a model is added to the decomposition set by an immune diagnosis, it cannot be removed even if the condition that triggered the addition resolves. FOLLOW: In a long session where a model temporarily underperforms (transient API issues, rate limiting), the immune layer adds it to decomposition. When the model recovers, it remains in the decomposition set permanently, receiving unnecessarily decomposed tasks for the rest of the session. This degrades throughput and wastes tokens on a model that no longer needs decomposition.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add a `remove_from_decomposition(model_id)` path gated on sustained recovery (e.g., N consecutive rounds without the triggering failure condition), subject to the same P-pass gate and damping rules as addition.

all_findings.description: FIND: The interface summary (Section 2) lists `self._deferred_remediations` as write-only state where remediations rejected by the P-pass gate are logged. No retry, re-evaluation, or escalation interface is documented. DeepSeek_IM_F008 identified the ambiguity of what happens when `p_pass_remediation` returns False, but the downstream question is also unanswered: are deferred remediations ever retried in subsequent rounds when conditions change? FOLLOW: If a remediation is deferred because the metric hasn't degraded enough, but the metric continues to degrade over subsequent rounds, the system should re-attempt the deferred remediation. Without a retry mechanism, deferred remediations are silently dropped, and the immune layer loses its only record of a needed-but-blocked action.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add a `review_deferred_remediations(round)` call in `process_round()` that re-evaluates deferred items against current metrics each round. Items that now pass the P-pass gate are applied; items that have been deferred for more than N rounds without the triggering condition resolving are escalated to a higher-severity remediation or logged as unresolvable.

all_findings.description: FIND: The immune layer can modify `tau_sim` and `tau_vocab_growth` (convergence/vocabulary thresholds). The `diminishing_returns.stop(r)` signal depends on "exhaustion AND abstraction_ok" — vocabulary growth rate (influenced by `tau_vocab_growth`) feeds into this. The damping mechanism (`immune_damping_rounds = 2`) only prevents rapid re-adjustment of the *same parameter*. It does not prevent a cross-detector feedback loop: immune lowers `tau_vocab_growth` → DR detector's `vocab_growth_rate(r)` now reports saturation sooner → `stop(r)` fires earlier → session terminates prematurely → immune never observes the rounds that would have shown the threshold was too aggressive. FOLLOW: This is a classic control-loop instability. The immune layer acts as a controller modifying setpoints of two coupled detectors without a stability constraint across them. DeepSeek_IM_F009 identified the convergence-detector mid-stream issue but did not identify this DR-detector coupling.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Either (a) extend damping to be cross-parameter: after any threshold adjustment, impose a cooldown on all threshold parameters (not just the one adjusted), or (b) add a monotonicity guard: threshold adjustments must move in the permissive direction only (lowering thresholds makes convergence/stop easier to reach, which is safe; raising them is the dangerous direction that extends sessions).

all_findings.description: FIND: The interface summary Section 4 ("Dataclasses/Types Used Across Boundary") omits `FailureRecord` despite it being imported by the shim from `_types.py` and being the obvious output type of `FailureHandler` (an immune boundary component). Every other type relevant to the immune boundary is listed. FOLLOW: A reviewer using the interface summary as their sole reference for cross-boundary types will not know `FailureRecord` exists, its schema, or where it flows. This is a documentation completeness defect in the review package, not in the code.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add `FailureRecord` to Section 4 with its line number, fields, and role in the immune subsystem (output of `FailureHandler`, input to remediation chain selection).

all_findings.description:
FIND: The Interface Summary Section 2 lists `self.config.per_model_directives` as mutable state that the immune subsystem writes, but does not specify any constraints on the directive content beyond the `max_per_model_directive_chars` config parameter. Missing constraints:  
- Are directives plain text, structured JSON, or a specific template?  
- Can they contain newlines, special characters, or markup?  
- Is there a validation function that rejects malformed directives?  
Without these constraints, the immune subsystem could inject directives that cause parsing failures or prompt‑injection vulnerabilities in the model‑calling layer.  

FIX:  
Add to Interface Summary Section 3 (Config Parameters) or as a new subsection “Directive Constraints”:  

| Constraint | Requirement |  
|------------|-------------|  
| Format | Plain text; no HTML/XML tags, no JSON structures unless explicitly escaped |  
| Encoding | UTF‑8, no control characters except `\n`, `\t` |  
| Validation | `validate_directive(text)` returns `True` if `len(text) ≤ max_per_model_directive_chars` and contains no forbidden sequences (e.g., `\0`, `\r`, `"""` triple‑quotes) |  
| Injection safety | Directives are appended with a clear separator (`\n\n---\n`) to avoid prompt‑smuggling |  

FOLLOW:  
1. The immune subsystem’s directive‑injection transforms (`add_synthesis_directive`, etc.) must call `validate_directive` before writing to `per_model_directives`.  
2. The model‑calling layer must be updated to handle the specified separator and encoding.  
3. Any existing directives in the config must be audited for compliance; non‑compliant directives could break model responses silently.  

---

all_findings.description: FIND: Interface Summary Section 2 lists `self._pre_fix_snapshots` as write-only mutable state ("Pre-adjustment config snapshots"). No interface function in any section reads, restores, or consumes these snapshots. FOLLOW: The existence of snapshots implies a rollback capability — you only snapshot state if you intend to restore it on failure. But the interface summary documents no rollback path: no `restore_snapshot()`, no conditional revert in `apply_diagnosis()`, no consumer in `process_round()`. This means either (a) rollback exists but is undocumented, making the interface summary incomplete for a critical safety path, or (b) rollback does not exist, making the snapshots write-only dead state that creates a false impression of recoverability.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Document the rollback mechanism in the interface summary — specifically, what triggers a restore, what function performs it, and whether rollback is atomic or partial. If no rollback exists, remove `_pre_fix_snapshots` or document it as audit-only with an explicit note that it does not provide revert capability.

all_findings.description: FIND: Interface Summary Section 2 lists `self._deferred_remediations` as write-only mutable state. Section 1 shows `health_monitor.p_pass_remediation()` returns `(approved, reason)`, and prior finding DeepSeek_IM_F008 flags the unanswered question of what happens when `approved=False`. The missing piece that DeepSeek_IM_F008 did not identify: `_deferred_remediations` has no documented drain mechanism. No interface function re-evaluates, retries, escalates, or clears deferred remediations in subsequent rounds. FOLLOW: Without a drain, deferred remediations accumulate indefinitely. If a remediation is deferred because conditions aren't right in round N, but conditions improve by round N+3, the system has no mechanism to revisit it. The immune layer can detect problems and propose fixes but has no path to re-attempt fixes that were correctly deferred. This is a completeness gap in the immune feedback loop — it can defer but never un-defer.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add a drain/retry interface: either `apply_diagnosis()` should re-evaluate `_deferred_remediations` each round against current metrics, or a separate `retry_deferred_remediations(round, metrics)` function should exist in the interface summary with its trigger conditions documented.

all_findings.description: FIND: The shim exports `State` and `Event` types from `_types.py` (presumably enums given their naming and placement alongside other enums like `FailureType`, `RecoveryAction`). However, Interface Summary Section 1 defines `fsm.select_event()` as returning `str` and `fsm.transition(event)` as accepting `str` and returning `str`. FOLLOW: If `State` and `Event` are enums, the FSM interface operates on raw strings rather than the typed enums, defeating type safety at the immune/FSM boundary. The immune layer's `process_round()` calls `fsm.select_event()` and `fsm.transition()` — if these return strings that must be compared to `State`/`Event` enum members, every call site is an implicit `str→enum` conversion point without a documented contract for how that conversion works or what happens on mismatch. If `State` and `Event` are not enums but type aliases for `str`, then their export as named types is misleading.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Align the FSM interface signatures with the exported types: `fsm.select_event(...) → Event` and `fsm.transition(event: Event) → State`. Update the interface summary to reflect typed signatures. If the FSM intentionally uses raw strings, document why and remove the typed exports or alias them explicitly.

For the immune boundary specifically: if `FindingEquivalenceClass` is used by `DetectorDiagnosis` or the convergence/similarity logic that feeds immune decisions, its omission from the interface means reviewers cannot trace how finding equivalence affects immune behaviour.

all_findings.description: FIND: The shim exports `ManagerEventStream` from `_events.py` as a separate section. Interface Summary Section 1 shows `FailureHandler` (within immune boundary) calls `event_callback(event)` with signature `(ManagerEvent) → None`. The relationship between `ManagerEventStream` and `event_callback` is undocumented. FOLLOW: Is `event_callback` a method of `ManagerEventStream`? A closure provided by it? A standalone function? The immune layer depends on this callback for observability — if `FailureHandler` emits events through a mechanism whose contract is undefined, the event delivery guarantee is unknown. Can events be dropped? Are they buffered? Is the callback synchronous (blocking immune execution) or asynchronous? For an immune subsystem that must detect and respond to failures, silent event loss means silent observability loss, which means failures in the immune layer itself go undetected.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Document in the interface summary: (a) what object provides `event_callback` to `FailureHandler`, (b) delivery guarantee (at-least-once, best-effort), (c) whether the callback is synchronous or asynchronous, (d) failure mode if the callback itself raises.

all_findings.description: FIND: Interface Summary Section 2 shows `self.config.pre_decompose_models` as a `Set[str]` with R/W access for the immune subsystem ("Immune can add models to decomposition set"). No removal mechanism is documented. FOLLOW: If the immune layer adds a model to `pre_decompose_models` due to underperformance in round N, but the model recovers in later rounds (e.g., after a directive injection or retry), the model remains in the decomposition set permanently. Over a long session, this set grows monotonically. Decomposition presumably adds overhead (splitting tasks for weaker models); permanently decomposing a recovered model is a resource waste that compounds. This is an edge case in the immune feedback loop: the immune system can escalate (add to decomposition) but cannot de-escalate (remove from decomposition when evidence warrants).
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add a de-escalation path: either `apply_diagnosis()` should evaluate whether models in `pre_decompose_models` still need decomposition based on current `capability_scores`, or document an explicit design decision that decomposition is permanent with rationale (e.g., conservative safety stance).

all_findings.description: FIND: The CDSFL distributed-systems hard constraint requires monotonic clocks for elapsed-time measurement: "Use monotonic clocks for elapsed time... Wall clocks are for human display only." The Interface Summary shows `timeout_multiplier` (line 149) as an immune config parameter for failure detection, and `FailureType.TIMEOUT` as a failure classification. The timeout detection mechanism necessarily measures elapsed time between request dispatch and response receipt. Neither the interface summary nor the shim documents which clock source is used for this measurement. FOLLOW: If `FailureHandler` uses wall-clock time (`time.time()`, `datetime.now()`, etc.), NTP step corrections can cause false positives (clock jumps forward → spurious timeout) or false negatives (clock jumps backward → missed timeout). In an immune subsystem whose purpose is reliable failure detection, a non-monotonic clock source directly undermines correctness.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Specify in the interface summary or `FailureHandler` contract that timeout measurement must use `time.monotonic()` (or equivalent monotonic source). Verify the implementation uses monotonic time, not wall-clock time.

all_findings.description: FIND: The shim establishes a flat re-export namespace where all submodules are importable from a single path (`from dynamic_management import X`). Python's import machinery can handle some circular cases at module level but fails when the circularly-imported name hasn't been bound yet at import time. The immune layer is at highest risk because `_manager.py` orchestrates all immune components and is the last submodule imported in the shim. No guard exists: no documentation warning, no runtime assertion, and no `__all__` to signal the intended import direction. PROPOSED_FIX: (1) Add a comment at the top of the shim: "Submodules must NOT import from this file — import from peer submodules directly." (2) Add a CI lint rule or import-order check that flags any `from dynamic_management import` inside `bench/dm/`. (3) Define `__all__` to make the intended public surface explicit and discourage casual use of the shim as an internal import source.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, there is no explicit public grouping or alias for the immune subsystem even though the file is being used as a compatibility surface for a decomposed monolith. The immune API is scattered across four blocks: `_types` (`DetectorDiagnosis`, enums, result types), `_immune` (`DetectorHealthMonitor`), `_failure_handler` (`FailureHandler`, `CorrelatedFailureModel`), and `_manager` (only `DynamicManager`, despite the docstring naming other immune symbols). This is a missed interface defect at the shim level: a caller cannot determine immune API completeness by inspecting one section because immune-relevant names are fragmented and partially hidden behind generic headings. Evidence: the “Immune layer” block does not include `DetectorDiagnosis` even though it is in-scope, and the orchestrator block does not expose the immune orchestration helpers named in the inventory.  
FIX: Reorganize the shim imports so the immune public surface is declared contiguously and explicitly. Exact replacement for the immune/orchestrator-related blocks:  
<<<<
# ── Immune layer ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._immune import DetectorHealthMonitor  # noqa: F401
from bench.dm._failure_handler import (  # noqa: F401
    FailureHandler,
    CorrelatedFailureModel,
)

# ── Event stream ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._events import ManagerEventStream  # noqa: F401

# ── Orchestrator ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._manager import DynamicManager  # noqa: F401
====
# ── Immune layer ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Public immune API spans shared types, detector health, failure handling,
# and manager remediation/orchestration hooks.
from bench.dm._immune import DetectorHealthMonitor  # noqa: F401
from bench.dm._failure_handler import (  # noqa: F401
    FailureHandler,
    CorrelatedFailureModel,
)
from bench.dm._manager import (  # noqa: F401
    DynamicManager,
    _REMEDIATION_CHAINS,
    apply_diagnosis,
    _apply_transform,
)

# ── Event stream ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._events import ManagerEventStream  # noqa: F401
>>>>
FOLLOW: This fix has two downstream consequences. First, it makes the shim’s section structure consistent with the analytical boundary, reducing the chance of accidental omission during future refactors. Second, if `_manager.py` does not actually expose `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS`, `apply_diagnosis`, or `_apply_transform` at module scope, this import will fail, revealing a deeper export/ownership bug rather than silently masking it. That failure would be desirable because the current shim already advertises those symbols in documentation.

all_findings.description: FIND: `FailureRecord` is imported from `_types` and re-exported by the shim, but is absent from Interface Summary Section 4 (Dataclasses/Types Used Across Boundary). The interface summary lists `FailureType` (enum) and `RecoveryAction` (enum) but not `FailureRecord`, despite `FailureHandler` being a core immune-boundary component that logically produces failure records. all_findings.description: FIND: The shim is a backward-compatibility migration aid but contains no deprecation signal — no `warnings.warn("Import from bench.dm.* instead", DeprecationWarning)`, no `__deprecated__` markers, no documented migration timeline. Every future change to the immune subsystem must verify both the submodule path and the shim re-export path, with no visibility into which consumers use which. This is distinct from the `__all__` finding (which concerns export surface control) — this concerns the shim's lifecycle.

Document the migration timeline in the module docstring.

If it is used only by convergence/DR detectors outside the immune boundary: document that explicitly so reviewers don't waste time tracing a non-existent dependency.

all_findings.description: FIND: The shim exposes `State` and `Event` from `_types.py`, while the interface summary types them inconsistently as plain `str` in the FSM calls: `fsm.select_event(...) -> str` and `fsm.transition(event) -> str`. In a backward-compatible shim, exported types are part of the external contract. If callers use `Event`/`State` enums but the interface and downstream methods are documented as `str`, the immune integration in `process_round()` sits on an under-specified interface boundary: comparisons, serialization, and logging may break depending on whether code uses enum members or raw strings. This is a genuine interface defect in the supplied materials and is not duplicated by prior findings about omitted types; those findings targeted missing documentation of types, while this one is a concrete type contradiction between exported API and documented call signatures.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: Normalize the interface to use the exported types explicitly.

Replace the interface summary entries with:

<<<<
| `fsm.select_event(conv, dim, crit, complete)` | `(bool, bool, bool, bool) → str` | FSM event selection from round outcomes |
| `fsm.transition(event)` | `(str) → str` | FSM state transition, returns new state |
====
| `fsm.select_event(conv, dim, crit, complete)` | `(bool, bool, bool, bool) → Event` | FSM event selection from round outcomes |
| `fsm.transition(event)` | `(Event) → State` | FSM state transition, returns new state |
>>>>

If the implementation actually uses strings internally, then instead change the shim/types surface by removing `State` and `Event` from public export and documenting strings consistently. But one contract must win; both cannot be public truth at once.

FOLLOW: If this fix adopts typed `Event`/`State`, then all immune-boundary documentation and code touching FSM integration must be updated consistently:
- `process_round()` docs and annotations
- `RoundResult.state` type docs
- any `ManagerEvent` payloads that serialize FSM state/event
- any comparisons in tests that currently compare to string literals  
If this fix instead adopts strings, then `_types.py`, any enum serialization helpers, and the shim export surface must be reduced accordingly.

all_findings.description: FIND: The shim docstring hard-codes a stale monolith size: “6,890-line monolith,” while the verified facts for this task state `dynamic_management.py` is now approximately 6,100 lines. In a review-oriented compatibility shim, line-count claims are operational metadata used to justify decomposition and reviewability. A stale quantitative claim is documentation drift and undermines confidence in the refactor note that follows. This is separate from prior findings about overstated reviewability; here the defect is a specific false factual statement in the artifact.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: Remove the precise line-count claim or replace it with a non-brittle description.

<<<<
All classes, functions, and constants that were previously defined in this
6,890-line monolith are now in bench/dm/ submodules.
====
All classes, functions, and constants that were previously defined in the
original monolithic module are now in bench/dm/ submodules.
>>>>

FOLLOW: The same brittleness likely affects any other size/token-count claims in the docstring, especially the “~15-25K tokens” sentence. Those should be treated as advisory, not factual guarantees, or sourced from automated generation. No runtime downstream impact identified, but documentation consistency should be repaired together.

all_findings.description: FIND: The shim promises that “existing imports continue to work unchanged,” but its examples only demonstrate importing `DynamicManager` from two paths. For the immune layer specifically, the backward-compatibility claim is incomplete because the visible shim also re-exports `DetectorHealthMonitor`, `FailureHandler`, `CorrelatedFailureModel`, `FailureRecord`, and multiple enums/types. This is not the same as prior findings about missing examples for `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS` and manager helpers; the missed issue is that the examples fail to demonstrate compatibility for the actual immune classes that are successfully re-exported in the current artifact. That weakens the user-facing migration contract for the immune subsystem even where the shim does expose the names.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: Expand the docstring examples to cover immune-class imports that the shim actually supports.

<<<<
them so that existing imports continue to work unchanged:

    from dynamic_management import DynamicManager       # runners (bench/ CWD)
    from bench.dynamic_management import DynamicManager  # tests (repo root CWD)
====
them so that existing imports continue to work unchanged:

    from dynamic_management import DynamicManager, DetectorHealthMonitor, FailureHandler
    from bench.dynamic_management import DynamicManager, DetectorHealthMonitor, FailureHandler
>>>>

FOLLOW: If these examples are added, the shim maintainers must ensure those imports remain stable in `__all__` or equivalent explicit export control; otherwise the examples become another drifting promise. This strengthens the case for a pinned export surface, but does not by itself require runtime code changes beyond documentation unless `__all__` is added.

all_findings.description: FIND: `CorrelatedFailureModel` is exported from `_failure_handler.py` under the shim's "Immune layer" section, establishing it as part of the immune public surface. However, the Interface Summary — which is the sole specification provided for immune behaviour — never references `CorrelatedFailureModel` in any function signature (Section 1), shared mutable state (Section 2), config parameter (Section 3), or cross-boundary type table (Section 4). FOLLOW: This creates a verification dead zone. Either (a) `CorrelatedFailureModel` has runtime contracts with `FailureHandler` or `DetectorHealthMonitor` that the interface summary fails to document — meaning the immune specification is incomplete for any model that detects correlated failures, or (b) it is dead code within the immune boundary, exported but unused. A reviewer cannot distinguish these cases from the provided artifact and summary alone. The practical consequence: if correlated failure detection influences `RecoveryAction` selection (e.g., choosing `EXCLUDE` over `RETRY` when failures are correlated across models), that decision logic is invisible to review.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add `CorrelatedFailureModel` to Interface Summary Section 4 with its constructor signature, the immune-layer functions that consume it, and the behavioural contract it fulfils (e.g., input to `FailureHandler` correlation detection). If it is internal-only to `_failure_handler.py`, remove it from the shim's public immune exports.

all_findings.description: FIND: `FailureRecord` is imported and re-exported from `_types.py` in the shim, but it is completely absent from Interface Summary Section 4 ("Dataclasses/Types Used Across Boundary"), despite `FailureHandler` being a core immune-boundary component that logically produces failure records. FOLLOW: The interface summary documents `FailureType` (enum of failure categories) and `RecoveryAction` (enum of responses), but omits the dataclass that presumably binds them together with contextual data (model ID, round, timestamp, failure details). If `FailureRecord` crosses the immune boundary — e.g., stored in shared state, passed to `role_assignment.record_failure`, or logged in `_immune_adjustments` — then its schema is an undocumented contract. Downstream consumers (health monitor, remediation chains) cannot be verified against a type they cannot see.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add `FailureRecord` to Interface Summary Section 4 with its fields and which immune-boundary functions produce/consume it. If it is boundary-internal, document that and consider removing it from the public shim.

all_findings.description: FIND: The shim's "Immune layer" section imports only `DetectorHealthMonitor` from `_immune.py` and `FailureHandler`/`CorrelatedFailureModel` from `_failure_handler.py`. But `DetectorDiagnosis` — the return type of the health monitor's core diagnostic operation, used by `apply_diagnosis()` to drive remediation — is sourced from `_types.py` in a completely separate import group with no cross-reference. FOLLOW: A consumer who reads the shim as an API guide and imports only from the "Immune layer" grouping gets the immune *actors* but not the immune *output type* needed to type-check their interactions. This is distinct from the prior finding (ChatGPT_IM_F009) that noted the sourcing difference: the issue here is that the shim's section boundaries create a false impression of self-contained immune imports. In practice, `DetectorHealthMonitor` → produces `DetectorDiagnosis` → consumed by `apply_diagnosis()` on `DynamicManager` (sourced from "Orchestrator" section). The immune call chain spans three shim sections with no documentation connecting them.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add a brief inline comment in the immune section: `# DetectorDiagnosis (return type of health_monitor.diagnose) is in _types.py above`. Alternatively, add `DetectorDiagnosis` as a secondary import in the immune section (aliased or commented) to make the dependency explicit.

all_findings.description: FIND: `FindingEquivalenceClass` is exported from `_types.py` by the shim but does not appear anywhere in the Interface Summary (Sections 1–4). The immune layer's `DetectorHealthMonitor` plausibly uses equivalence classes to group findings for health assessment and remediation targeting — the interface summary shows `health_monitor.recommended_chain_start(key)` where `key` is a string, and equivalence classes would be a natural source of those keys. FOLLOW: If `FindingEquivalenceClass` is the mechanism by which the immune layer maps findings to remediation chains, its absence from the interface specification means the key-generation logic is undocumented. A reviewer cannot verify whether the `key` parameter in `recommended_chain_start(key)` and `record_chain_exhaustion(key)` is derived from `FindingEquivalenceClass` identifiers, flaw_class enums, or something else entirely.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Document `FindingEquivalenceClass` in Interface Summary Section 4 if it participates in immune-boundary interactions. Specify the relationship between equivalence class identifiers and the `key` parameter used by `health_monitor` methods.

all_findings.description: FIND: The shim's import order places immune-layer modules (`_immune.py`, `_failure_handler.py`) after all area implementations (`_convergence.py`, `_diminishing_returns.py`, `_fsm.py`, etc.). The Interface Summary shows the immune layer has runtime dependencies on convergence_detector, diminishing_returns, fsm, and role_assignment. In Python, if any of these modules have import-time side effects (e.g., module-level registrations, singleton initialisation, or metaclass operations), the shim's import ordering implicitly encodes a dependency graph that is nowhere documented. FOLLOW: This is fragile for a backward-compatibility shim: an automated tool reordering imports alphabetically or by section would silently break any import-time dependency. The original monolith had no import-ordering concern because all definitions were in one file. The refactored shim inherits implicit ordering constraints that the monolith did not have, and documents none of them.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add a comment block at the top of the shim documenting the required import ordering and why it matters (or, if no import-time dependencies exist, document that ordering is arbitrary). Better: ensure no module in `bench/dm/` has import-time side effects, making ordering genuinely irrelevant, and document that invariant.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, module docstring vs actual exports, immune boundary packaging. The shim says “All classes, functions, and constants that were previously defined in this 6,890-line monolith are now in bench/dm/ submodules” and specifically states `_manager.py` contains immune-orchestrator symbols `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS`, `apply_diagnosis`, `_apply_transform`, and `process_round`. In the actual import section, only `DynamicManager` is imported from `bench.dm._manager`; none of those named module-level immune symbols are re-exported. This is a concrete interface mismatch in the artifact itself, not a behavioural inference. Evidence: the only orchestrator import is `from bench.dm._manager import DynamicManager`, so `from dynamic_management import apply_diagnosis` and `from dynamic_management import _REMEDIATION_CHAINS` cannot work through this shim.
FIX: Replace the orchestrator import with an explicit re-export of the named immune manager symbols.
<<<<
# ── Orchestrator ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._manager import DynamicManager  # noqa: F401
====
# ── Orchestrator ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._manager import (  # noqa: F401
    DynamicManager,
    _REMEDIATION_CHAINS,
    apply_diagnosis,
    _apply_transform,
    process_round,
)
>>>>
FOLLOW: This fix changes the shim’s public surface and must be propagated to any explicit export control. Because this file currently has no `__all__`, adding these imports makes them publicly discoverable via attribute access but still leaves the API implicit. That reveals a second issue: the shim should define `__all__` so the newly restored immune symbols are part of a stable, intentional compatibility contract. No other downstream impact can be verified from the provided artifact alone.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Explicitly import and re-export `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS`, `apply_diagnosis`, `_apply_transform`, and `process_round` from `bench.dm._manager` as shown above.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, immune-layer boundary statement in the module docstring is internally inconsistent with the same file’s imports. The docstring says: “The immune layer review boundary is: _types.py + _immune.py + _manager.py.” But the file’s own immune section imports `FailureHandler` and `CorrelatedFailureModel` from `_failure_handler.py`, and the user’s analytical boundary explicitly includes `FailureHandler`. This means the documented immune boundary omits a module that the shim itself treats as part of the immune layer. Evidence is direct text in the docstring plus the `from bench.dm._failure_handler import (...)` import block.
FIX: Correct the boundary statement to include `_failure_handler.py`.
<<<<
The immune layer review boundary is: _types.py + _immune.py + _manager.py.
====
The immune layer review boundary is: _types.py + _immune.py + _failure_handler.py + _manager.py.
>>>>
FOLLOW: This documentation fix also requires updating the module structure inventory so the immune section is consistently represented across all prose in the header. Specifically, the `_failure_handler.py` line should be annotated as part of the immune layer rather than left as an unqualified module listing. No code-path impact identified, but tooling or reviewers relying on the documented boundary would otherwise continue scoping reviews incorrectly.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Amend the boundary sentence exactly as shown so the documented immune review boundary matches the shim’s own imports.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, exported FSM contract is type-inconsistent with the provided interface summary. The shim exports `State` and `Event` from `bench.dm._types`, which implies callers are meant to use concrete FSM types. But the interface summary for the immune integration declares `fsm.select_event(...) -> str` and `fsm.transition(event) -> str`. That is a real interface contradiction at the boundary: either event/state are typed enums/classes, or they are raw strings. Both cannot be the stable external contract. Evidence: explicit export of `State, Event` in the shim and explicit `str` signatures in the supplied interface summary.
FIX: Correct the interface summary signatures to use the exported types.
<<<<
| `fsm.select_event(conv, dim, crit, complete)` | `(bool, bool, bool, bool) → str` | FSM event selection from round outcomes |
| `fsm.transition(event)` | `(str) → str` | FSM state transition, returns new state |
====
| `fsm.select_event(conv, dim, crit, complete)` | `(bool, bool, bool, bool) → Event` | FSM event selection from round outcomes |
| `fsm.transition(event)` | `(Event) → State` | FSM state transition, returns new state |
>>>>
FOLLOW: Once these signatures are corrected, all documentation and tests that currently treat FSM values as strings must be updated to use `Event` and `State`. That includes any immune logic in `process_round()` that serialises, compares, or logs FSM outputs as string literals. If string serialisation is still desired for events, the summary must document the conversion layer explicitly rather than flattening the type contract.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Replace the interface summary signatures with `Event`/`State` as shown above so they match the shim’s exported contract.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, module structure inventory is incomplete relative to the shim’s actual immune-relevant exports. The header says `_immune.py` contains “DetectorHealthMonitor (immune detection layer)” only, but the shim separately exports `DetectorDiagnosis` from `_types.py`, and the analytical boundary names `DetectorDiagnosis` as a first-class immune component. As written, the header fragments the diagnostic API across sections without documenting where the diagnosis object belongs in the immune subsystem. Evidence: `DetectorDiagnosis` is imported in the types block, while `_immune.py` is documented as if it exposes only the monitor. That makes the module inventory an incomplete specification of the immune surface.
FIX: Amend the module inventory to describe the diagnosis type as part of the immune-layer vocabulary.
<<<<
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses (all shared vocabulary)
    _immune.py             DetectorHealthMonitor (immune detection layer)
====
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses (all shared vocabulary,
                           including DetectorDiagnosis)
    _immune.py             DetectorHealthMonitor (immune detection layer)
>>>>
FOLLOW: This fix reduces ambiguity in the header, but it also highlights that the shim lacks any explicit grouping of immune exports. If reviewers or downstream callers need to know the full immune public surface, they still must infer it from dispersed imports. The stronger downstream fix is to add an `__all__` grouped by subsystem or a dedicated “Immune public API” comment block naming all boundary symbols.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Update the inventory text exactly as shown so `DetectorDiagnosis` is documented as immune-relevant shared vocabulary.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, compatibility shim has no explicit `__all__`, so the public API is an uncontrolled byproduct of top-level imports. In a backward-compatibility shim, especially one claiming continued support for prior imports, implicit export is an interface defect: adding or removing any import silently changes the supported surface. This matters directly to the immune subsystem because restoring missing symbols such as `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS` or `apply_diagnosis` would otherwise remain undocumented and unstable. Evidence: the file contains only import statements and no `__all__` declaration.
FIX: Add an explicit `__all__` enumerating the intended compatibility surface, including the immune symbols named in the docstring.
<<<<
from bench.dm._validation import validate_all_reductions  # noqa: F401
====
from bench.dm._validation import validate_all_reductions  # noqa: F401

__all__ = [
    "DynamicManagementConfig",
    "Role",
    "CapabilityFingerprint",
    "ModelSpec",
    "Task",
    "Finding",
    "FailureType",
    "RecoveryAction",
    "FailureRecord",
    "ModelResponse",
    "DetectorDiagnosis",
    "State",
    "Event",
    "TerminationReason",
    "ManagerEventType",
    "ManagerEvent",
    "RoundResult",
    "FindingEquivalenceClass",
    "RoleAssignment",
    "Allocation",
    "LoadBalancer",
    "RoundProgressionFSM",
    "ConvergenceDetector",
    "_finding_similarity",
    "_tokenize_for_similarity",
    "_bigrams",
    "_STOPWORDS",
    "DiminishingReturnsDetector",
    "DetectorHealthMonitor",
    "FailureHandler",
    "CorrelatedFailureModel",
    "ManagerEventStream",
    "DynamicManager",
    "_REMEDIATION_CHAINS",
    "apply_diagnosis",
    "_apply_transform",
    "process_round",
    "validate_all_reductions",
]
>>>>
FOLLOW: This fix depends on IM_F001 being applied first; otherwise `__all__` will name symbols not imported into the module and import-time failures will occur. It also forces an explicit decision on whether underscore-prefixed helpers like `_finding_similarity` and `_STOPWORDS` are intentionally public compatibility exports or accidental leakage. If they are not intended public API, they must be removed both from imports and from `__all__`.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add the explicit `__all__` block shown above after all imports.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, orchestrator import block plus module inventory. The docstring explicitly says `_manager.py` contains `DynamicManager (orchestrator, _REMEDIATION_CHAINS, apply_diagnosis, _apply_transform, process_round)`, but the shim imports only `DynamicManager` from `bench.dm._manager`. This is a distinct API break from the already-reported missing `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS` / `apply_diagnosis` / `_apply_transform`: `process_round` is also named as part of the preserved surface yet is not re-exported. Evidence in artifact: the only orchestrator import is `from bench.dm._manager import DynamicManager`, so `from dynamic_management import process_round` cannot work.  
FIX: Re-export the full documented orchestrator surface or correct the documentation to state these are methods/internal symbols, not top-level shim exports. Exact code replacement:
<<<<
# ── Orchestrator ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._manager import DynamicManager  # noqa: F401
====
# ── Orchestrator ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._manager import (  # noqa: F401
    DynamicManager,
    _REMEDIATION_CHAINS,
    apply_diagnosis,
    _apply_transform,
    process_round,
)
>>>>
FOLLOW: This fix requires corresponding updates to the public export contract. If `_manager.py` does not actually define module-level `apply_diagnosis`, `_apply_transform`, or `process_round` because they are `DynamicManager` methods, then the import will fail; in that case the docstring inventory is wrong and must be corrected everywhere it describes shim compatibility. This also interacts with the lack of `__all__`: after adding these names, `__all__` should be pinned so the intended API is explicit rather than incidental.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Re-export `process_round` together with the other documented `_manager.py` immune symbols, or revise the docstring to say they are `DynamicManager` methods and not shim-level exports.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, public import examples in the module docstring. The shim promises backward-compatible imports from both `dynamic_management` and `bench.dynamic_management`, but it only demonstrates `DynamicManager`. Within the immune boundary actually exposed by this file, there is a second import-path inconsistency: immune classes are re-exported at shim level (`DetectorHealthMonitor`, `FailureHandler`, `CorrelatedFailureModel`, `DetectorDiagnosis`), yet no examples show those supported imports. This is not the same as prior “examples only show DynamicManager” findings, because the concrete missed defect is that the compatibility guarantee is under-specified for the immune API surface actually present in this shim. Users cannot tell whether `from bench.dynamic_management import FailureHandler` is a supported compatibility path or an accidental side effect.  
FIX: Add explicit immune-surface examples beside the existing `DynamicManager` examples. Exact docstring replacement:
<<<<
them so that existing imports continue to work unchanged:

    from dynamic_management import DynamicManager       # runners (bench/ CWD)
    from bench.dynamic_management import DynamicManager  # tests (repo root CWD)
====
them so that existing imports continue to work unchanged:

    from dynamic_management import DynamicManager
    from bench.dynamic_management import DynamicManager

    # Immune-layer compatibility imports also remain supported:
    from dynamic_management import DetectorHealthMonitor, FailureHandler, DetectorDiagnosis
    from bench.dynamic_management import DetectorHealthMonitor, FailureHandler, DetectorDiagnosis
>>>>
FOLLOW: If maintainers do not want these immune imports to be part of the public compatibility contract, then the correct downstream action is the opposite: stop re-exporting them and narrow the shim API. As written, though, the code does re-export them, so the documentation should match. This also increases pressure to define `__all__`, because examples without explicit export control still leave the public surface ambiguous.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Extend the docstring examples to include immune-layer imports on both supported paths.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, module structure inventory versus actual imports. The inventory labels `_immune.py` as `DetectorHealthMonitor (immune detection layer)`, while `DetectorDiagnosis` is imported from `_types.py`. That creates an undocumented split of the immune diagnosis contract across two modules: the detector implementation is in `_immune.py`, but its core diagnosis payload type lives elsewhere. This is a boundary-spec completeness defect, not just a naming nit, because the task boundary explicitly includes `DetectorDiagnosis`. A reviewer or downstream maintainer using the inventory alone would inspect `_immune.py` and miss one of the boundary’s key types.  
FIX: Amend the inventory to show that the immune boundary spans both `_types.py` and `_immune.py` for diagnosis data and logic. Exact docstring replacement:
<<<<
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses (all shared vocabulary)
    _role_assignment.py    RoleAssignment (Area 1)
    _load_balancer.py      Allocation, LoadBalancer (Area 2)
    _fsm.py                RoundProgressionFSM (Area 3)
    _convergence.py        ConvergenceDetector, finding similarity (Area 4)
    _diminishing_returns.py DiminishingReturnsDetector (Area 5)
    _immune.py             DetectorHealthMonitor (immune detection layer)
====
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses, DetectorDiagnosis
    _role_assignment.py    RoleAssignment (Area 1)
    _load_balancer.py      Allocation, LoadBalancer (Area 2)
    _fsm.py                RoundProgressionFSM (Area 3)
    _convergence.py        ConvergenceDetector, finding similarity (Area 4)
    _diminishing_returns.py DiminishingReturnsDetector (Area 5)
    _immune.py             DetectorHealthMonitor (immune detection logic)
>>>>
FOLLOW: Once this is corrected, the final sentence defining the review boundary should remain consistent with it. If the review boundary includes `DetectorDiagnosis`, then either `_types.py` must stay in scope explicitly or `DetectorDiagnosis` should be relocated into `_immune.py`. Otherwise the decomposition guide continues to misdirect reviewers.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Update the module inventory so `DetectorDiagnosis` is explicitly documented as part of the immune boundary via `_types.py`.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, module docstring sentence “All classes, functions, and constants that were previously defined in this 6,890-line monolith are now in bench/dm/ submodules.” This claim is stronger than what the shim demonstrates, because the file does not verify or enumerate “all” prior symbols and in fact its own imports omit some `_manager.py` symbols named in the inventory. The issue here is the absolute wording “all,” which is false on the face of the artifact provided.  
FIX: Replace the absolute claim with a scoped, supportable statement. Exact docstring replacement:
<<<<
All classes, functions, and constants that were previously defined in this
6,890-line monolith are now in bench/dm/ submodules. This file re-exports
them so that existing imports continue to work unchanged:
====
Core classes, functions, and constants from the former monolith are now in
bench/dm/ submodules. This file re-exports the supported compatibility surface
so that existing imports can continue to work unchanged:
>>>>
FOLLOW: After weakening this statement, the code should define the “supported compatibility surface” explicitly via `__all__`; otherwise the replacement text still lacks a concrete source of truth. This also reduces contradiction with the missing orchestrator exports identified above.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Remove the unsupported universal claim and describe the shim as re-exporting a defined supported surface.

all_findings.description:
FIND: The analytical boundary explicitly includes “immune config parameters,” but the only config symbol re-exported is the aggregate `DynamicManagementConfig`. The docstring never maps the immune parameters listed in the interface summary (`immune_feedback_enabled`, `immune_damping_rounds`, `max_per_model_directive_chars`, `timeout_multiplier`, `theta_under`, `n_fail`, `persistence_window`, `eta_underperform`, `k_min`) to that config type. This is a specification completeness defect at the boundary: the shim exposes the container but not the contract for the immune knobs the task says are in scope.  
FIX: Add a one-line inventory annotation tying immune parameters to `DynamicManagementConfig`. Exact docstring replacement:
<<<<
    _types.py              Config, enums, dataclasses, DetectorDiagnosis
====
    _types.py              DynamicManagementConfig (including immune parameters),
                           enums, dataclasses, DetectorDiagnosis
>>>>
FOLLOW: This does not expose the individual fields programmatically; it only fixes the boundary documentation. If backward compatibility for direct field access is important, then the underlying `DynamicManagementConfig` definition should also document these fields in its class docstring or type comments. Otherwise reviewers still have to infer immune configuration from external summaries.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Document in the shim inventory that immune config parameters live on `DynamicManagementConfig`.

all_findings.description:
FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, import organization. The shim groups `FailureHandler` under “Immune layer” but groups `ManagerEventStream` separately under “Event stream,” despite the interface summary showing an immediate dependency: `FailureHandler` calls `event_callback(event)` with `ManagerEvent`. This split obscures a direct adjacent dependency inside the immune boundary. The defect is not that eventing exists, but that ownership is mis-framed: a reviewer following the section headers can wrongly treat `_events.py` as out-of-bound support code even though immune behaviour depends on it.  
FIX: Mark the event stream section as an immune-adjacent dependency in the shim comments. Exact code replacement:
<<<<
# ── Event stream ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from bench.dm._events import ManagerEventStream  # noqa: F401
====
# ── Event stream (immune-adjacent dependency via FailureHandler callbacks) ──
from bench.dm._events import ManagerEventStream  # noqa: F401
>>>>
FOLLOW: This is documentation-only, but it affects review scoping and debugging. If the project wants strict architectural boundaries, a stronger downstream fix would be to add this dependency to the analytical boundary or interface summary explicitly; otherwise failures in event emission remain easy to misclassify as “outside immune.”
all_findings.proposed_fix: Relabel the event-stream import block to reflect its direct immune dependency.

all_findings.description: FIND: The Mathematical Appendix (Artifact 2) is a theoretical extension, not the immune‑layer implementation. The Detection sub‑area of immune (DetectorHealthMonitor, FailureHandler, etc.) is specified in the analytical boundary but absent from the review artifact. The appendix introduces advanced detection models (e.g., Duane NHPP, Abstraction Index, NMI diversity, seeded defect injection) that the immune layer may or may not implement. Without the actual source code (_immune.py, _failure_handl

FIND: `_deferred_remediations` (Interface Summary §2) is write-only with no documented consumer or re-evaluation path. When `health_monitor.p_pass_remediation()` returns `(False, reason)`, the remediation is logged to `_deferred_remediations`. But no interface exists to re-attempt deferred remediations in subsequent rounds. The list grows monotonically and is never drained. FOLLOW: This means a remediation that is deferred in round N due to insufficient evidence is permanently abandoned — even if later rounds produce the evidence that would justify it. The immune system can detect a problem, propose a fix, have it gated, and then never revisit it. For chronic low-severity issues that only cross the p_pass threshold after accumulating evidence over multiple rounds, the fix is structurally unreachable. This is a silent completeness failure: the system looks like it has a safety gate, but the gate is a one-way door to oblivion.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add a re-evaluation sweep in `process_round()` that iterates `_deferred_remediations` after each round's new data is available, re-submitting each deferred remediation to `p_pass_remediation()` with updated metrics. Remediations that pass are applied; those that fail are retained with an updated attempt count and timestamp. Add a maximum deferral age or attempt count after which the remediation is either escalated or explicitly dropped with a logged rationale.

all_findings.description: FIND: `_pre_fix_snapshots` (Interface Summary §2) is write-only with no rollback interface. The immune subsystem captures config state before applying adjustments, but no interface method consumes these snapshots to restore prior state. FOLLOW: The snapshots serve no operational purpose without a rollback trigger. If an immune adjustment degrades performance (e.g., lowering `tau_sim` causes premature convergence), there is no mechanism to detect the degradation and revert. The snapshot list consumes memory proportional to the number of adjustments made but provides zero recovery capability. This is dead infrastructure — it looks like a safety mechanism but cannot function as one.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Implement a rollback evaluator that compares post-adjustment round metrics against the pre-fix snapshot baseline. If metrics degrade beyond a threshold within a configurable observation window (e.g., 2 rounds post-adjustment), automatically restore the snapshot and log the rollback. Expose a `rollback(snapshot_index)` method on `DynamicManager` and document the trigger conditions.

all_findings.description: FIND: `self.capability_scores` (Interface Summary §2) is listed as R/W shared mutable state that the immune subsystem writes, but it is not a config parameter — it is runtime state on `DynamicManager`. The `immune_damping_rounds` constraint (line 168) applies to "same parameter" adjustments, where "parameter" reasonably means config fields like `tau_sim` or `tau_vocab_growth`. Capability score mutations are not config parameter adjustments and therefore bypass the damping mechanism entirely. FOLLOW: The immune subsystem can degrade a model's capability scores every single round without any damping delay. If a model has a transient failure (e.g., one timeout due to provider latency), the immune system can compound score penalties across consecutive rounds before the model has a chance to demonstrate recovery. This creates a positive feedback loop: lower scores → worse role assignments → worse performance → lower scores. The damping mechanism was designed to prevent exactly this kind of oscillation, but it doesn't cover the primary feedback channel.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Extend `immune_damping_rounds` to cover capability score adjustments per model, or introduce a separate `capability_score_damping_rounds` parameter. The damping check should key on `(model_id, "capability_scores")` in the same tracking structure used for config parameter damping.

all_findings.description: FIND: `process_round()` feeds data to both `convergence_detector` and `diminishing_returns`, then passes their boolean outputs to `fsm.select_event(conv, dim, crit, complete)`. The interface summary shows `convergence_detector.converged(r)` and `diminishing_returns.stop(r)` can produce contradictory signals: converged=True but stop=False (system appears converged but diminishing returns detector says continue), or converged=False but stop=True (not converged but DR says stop). FOLLOW: `fsm.select_event()` receives both booleans but no precedence rule is documented in the interface. The FSM event selection is a black box at this interface boundary. If `stop=True` triggers a terminal FSM event while `converged=False`, the system halts before convergence — potentially dropping findings. If `converged=True` is ignored because `stop=False`, the system wastes rounds. The immune subsystem's threshold adjustments to `tau_sim` and `tau_vocab_growth` directly influence these signals, so an immune adjustment can create a contradictory state that the FSM resolves in an undocumented way.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Document the precedence semantics in `fsm.select_event()`: does convergence override diminishing returns, or vice versa? Add the precedence rule to the interface summary. If both signals are inputs to a priority encoder, specify the truth table explicitly. At minimum: `(conv=True, stop=True)` → converge; `(conv=False, stop=True)` → stop with warning; `(conv=True, stop=False)` → converge; `(conv=False, stop=False)` → continue.

all_findings.description: FIND: `health_monitor.set_remediation_state(key, idx, round, metric, target)` records remediation chain progress, and `immune_damping_rounds` can block the actual config adjustment in the same or subsequent round. These two mechanisms operate independently. FOLLOW: If the immune subsystem calls `set_remediation_state` to record that chain step `idx` was reached, then attempts the actual adjustment but is blocked by damping, the health monitor's internal state says "step idx applied in round N" while the config remains unchanged. On the next round, `recommended_chain_start(key)` returns `idx+1`, skipping the step that was never actually applied. The remediation chain advances through its steps without the corresponding config changes taking effect. This is a state divergence between the health monitor's model of reality and actual system state.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Call `set_remediation_state` only *after* the adjustment is confirmed applied (i.e., after the damping check passes and the config is mutated). If damping blocks the adjustment, do not advance the chain state. Alternatively, make the damping check part of `apply_diagnosis()` before `set_remediation_state` is called, so the two are atomic from the chain's perspective.

all_findings.description: FIND: `FailureHandler` calls `event_callback(event)` with contract `(ManagerEvent) → None`. The return type `None` and the fire-and-forget signature mean FailureHandler has no mechanism to detect or handle callback failure. FOLLOW: If the event stream (ManagerEventStream) raises an exception during `event_callback`, the failure propagates into FailureHandler's own execution path. A failure *within the failure handler* — during the act of reporting a failure — is an unhandled edge case. Depending on where in FailureHandler's logic the callback is invoked (before or after recording the failure, before or after deciding the recovery action), a callback exception could leave FailureHandler's internal state inconsistent: failure detected but not recorded, or recorded but recovery action not emitted.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Wrap `event_callback(event)` in a try/except within FailureHandler that catches and logs callback failures without disrupting the failure-handling flow. The event callback is observational (logging/monitoring), not transactional — its failure must never compromise the primary failure-handling path.

all_findings.description: FIND: `CorrelatedFailureModel` is imported and re-exported under the "Immune layer" section of the shim, but it appears nowhere in the Interface Summary — not in §1 (external functions), §2 (shared state), §3 (config parameters), or §4 (types used across boundary). It has no documented methods, no documented inputs, and no documented role in the immune subsystem's decision-making. FOLLOW: This is distinct from prior findings about its public/private ambiguity. The issue is that it is an exported immune-layer component with zero interface documentation. Any consumer of `CorrelatedFailureModel` via this shim has no contract to code against. If it influences FailureHandler's escalation decisions (which the name implies — correlated failures across models should trigger different recovery than independent failures), that influence is entirely undocumented, making the immune subsystem's failure-correlation behaviour unverifiable at the interface level.
all_findings.proposed_fix: Add `CorrelatedFailureModel` to Interface Summary §4 with its type signature, or to §1 with its methods if FailureHandler delegates to it. If it is purely internal to `_failure_handler.py` and should not be part of the immune API surface, remove it from the shim's immune-layer export section.

all_findings.description: FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, module docstring sentence defining the review scope: `The immune layer review boundary is: _types.py + _immune.py + _manager.py.` This is internally inconsistent with the same file's actual immune exports and with the stated analytical boundary for this task. Independent observation 1: the shim re-exports `FailureHandler` and `CorrelatedFailureModel` from `bench.dm._failure_handler` under the `# ── Immune layer ──` section, so `_failure_handler.py` is part of the immune subsystem surface exposed by this file. Independent observation 2: the docstring's own module inventory lists `_failure_handler.py    FailureHandler, CorrelatedFailureModel`, confirming the module participates in the same decomposition the review boundary is describing. The result is a split-brain contract: consumers and reviewers are told one immune boundary while the public API exposes a larger one. This is cross-cutting because it affects review scope, import compatibility, and all immune behaviors that transit through `FailureHandler` before `process_round()` and `apply_diagnosis()` respond.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: Replace the boundary sentence with an exact boundary that matches the exported immune subsystem.
<<<< The immune layer review boundary is: _types.py + _immune.py + _manager.py. ==== The immune layer review boundary is: _types.py + _immune.py + _failure_handler.py + _manager.py. >>>>
FOLLOW: This fix requires the module inventory and any external review instructions to use the same four-module boundary. It also means immune-boundary interface summaries must document `FailureHandler`/`CorrelatedFailureModel` contracts alongside `DetectorHealthMonitor`, `apply_diagnosis()`, `_apply_transform()`, and `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS`; otherwise reviewers will still receive an incomplete contract package.

all_findings.description: FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, orchestrator import/export block versus the documented immune integration surface. The docstring explicitly states `_manager.py` contains `DynamicManager (orchestrator, _REMEDIATION_CHAINS, apply_diagnosis, _apply_transform, process_round)`, but the actual import line is only `from bench.dm._manager import DynamicManager`. Prior findings already covered missing re-exports for `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS`, `apply_diagnosis`, and `_apply_transform`; the missed issue is that `process_round` is also named as part of the old monolith surface yet is not made available at module scope. In a backward-compatible shim, naming a function in the compatibility inventory but only exposing it as an instance method is not equivalent compatibility. This matters across subsystems because `process_round()` is the integration point that ties immune diagnosis, convergence, diminishing returns, FSM transitions, failure recording, and fingerprint updates together. Any legacy code or tests that imported or monkey-patched `process_round` from the monolith namespace cannot do so through this shim.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: Re-export the manager-level symbols that the docstring claims are part of the compatibility surface, including `process_round`.
<<<< from bench.dm._manager import DynamicManager  # noqa: F401 ==== from bench.dm._manager import (  # noqa: F401
    DynamicManager,
    _REMEDIATION_CHAINS,
    apply_diagnosis,
    _apply_transform,
    process_round,
) >>>>
FOLLOW: After this change, the top-level API surface becomes consistent with the module inventory, but two downstream obligations appear. First, `__all__` should be added or updated so these names are intentionally public rather than accidental side effects of imports. Second, if `process_round` is no longer a module-level function in `_manager.py` but only a method on `DynamicManager`, then the docstring inventory is wrong and must be corrected instead; leaving both in place creates another interface contradiction.

all_findings.description: FIND: `dynamic_management.py`, import examples in the top docstring are materially incomplete for the immune subsystem. The file claims to be a backward-compatible shim for all previously defined classes, functions, and constants, but the only examples shown are `DynamicManager` imports from two package roots. Independent observation 1: this same shim publicly exposes multiple immune-specific names—`DetectorHealthMonitor`, `FailureHandler`, `CorrelatedFailureModel`, `DetectorDiagnosis`, `FailureRecord`, `ManagerEvent`, and `RoundResult`. Independent observation 2: the task's analytical boundary centers on immune behavior, not general orchestration. By documenting only `DynamicManager`, the shim leaves the immune import contract implicit and under-specified even though immune types span `_types.py`, `_immune.py`, `_failure_handler.py`, and `_manager.py`. This is a cross-cutting documentation defect because it obscures how the immune layer is supposed to be consumed from both runner and test contexts.
all_findings.proposed_fix:
FIX: Expand the examples block to include representative immune imports from both supported import roots.
<<<<     from dynamic_management import DynamicManager       # runners (bench/ CWD)
    from bench.dynamic_management import DynamicManager  # tests (repo root CWD) ====     from dynamic_management import DynamicManager, DetectorHealthMonitor, FailureHandler
    from bench.dynamic_management import (
        DynamicManager,
        DetectorHealthMonitor,
        FailureHandler,
        DetectorDiagnosis,
    ) >>>>
FOLLOW: Once these examples are added, the examples block will expose that manager-level immune helpers named in the inventory (`process_round`, `apply_diagnosis`, `_apply_transform`, `_REMEDIATION_CHAINS`) are still missing from the actual shim export unless IM_F025 is also applied. Without that companion fix, the examples become only partially representative of the documented immune API.
